title.name: The Green Men
title.subtitle: A mine through time
title.players: One miner, one mine through time
menu.easy.note: Bumps and bad air do less harm.
menu.normal.note: No clock: take your time and reach the cave at the bottom.
intro.1: Under Navarre lie mines from many ages. The deeper you dig, the further back in time you go.
intro.2: At the top, the 20th-century potash mine. Further down, the kings' iron, medieval copper and Roman galleries.
intro.3: And at the very bottom, the cave of the Green Men, the oldest miners of all. Can you reach them?
howto.title: How to play
howto.walk: Stick ← →: walk. Push into rock to dig
howto.dig: Stick ↓: dig down. You leave ladders behind you
howto.ladders: Stick ↑ ↓ on a ladder: climb. [B] puts a ladder where you stand
howto.light: Your light burns down underground: refill it at the lamp room (a little oil is free)
howto.sell: Ore sells itself at the weighbridge
howto.shop: [A] at the workshop: tools from every age, and where they lead
howto.danger: Mind loose rock, bad air and falls. If your light runs out, your workmates bring you up
help.play: ← → walk · ↓ dig · ↑↓ ladder · [B] place a ladder · [A] workshop

gl.title: Underground
gl.potasas.name: Potash of Navarre
gl.potasas.text: Here at Beriáin, potash was mined from 1963 to 1986. It was hard work, and it brought a whole mining town to life.
gl.potasa.name: Potash
gl.potasa.text: Reddish potassium salts. They make fertiliser that helps farm crops grow.
gl.hierro.name: Iron for the king
gl.hierro.text: At Eugi and Orbaizeta, iron from the hills was smelted with charcoal from the forests. Royal arms factories stood there.
gl.magnesita.name: Magnesite
gl.magnesita.text: A rock that stands enormous heat. It was found in the 1940s, when someone spotted pieces of it in the river Arga.
gl.cobre.name: The copper of the Arce valley
gl.cobre.text: Almost 700 years ago, the kings of Navarre looked for copper and silver in the Arce valley. They brought experts from far away, like Braccio from Florence.
gl.plata.name: Silver
gl.plata.text: Silver was made into coins. That is why kings wanted to know where to find it.
gl.romanos.name: Roman galleries
gl.romanos.text: About 2,000 years ago, the Romans cut galleries into the northern hills for silver and lead. Many of the people who worked there were not free.
gl.galena.name: Galena
gl.galena.text: It shines like metal. Lead and silver were made from it.
gl.moneda.name: A Roman coin
gl.moneda.text: Silver from the mines ended up as coins like this one.
gl.lucerna.name: A Roman lamp
gl.lucerna.text: The little oil lamp the Romans lit the galleries with.
gl.bronce.name: Bronze Age miners
gl.bronce.text: Thousands of years ago, people here broke the rock with fire and stone hammers to get copper. Their tools were made of stone and bone.
gl.malaquita.name: Malachite
gl.malaquita.text: A green stone, green because it holds copper. The first miners looked for it by its colour.
gl.hacha.name: A bronze axe
gl.hacha.text: Copper and tin melted together. The metal from the mines became tools.
gl.air.name: Bad air
gl.air.text: Underground, the air is sometimes not good to breathe. Miners learned to let fresh air into the tunnels.
gl.loose.name: Loose rock
gl.loose.text: Dig under loose rock and it falls. That is why miners propped up their tunnels with timber.
gl.escalera.name: Ladders
gl.escalera.text: The first miners climbed notched tree trunks. Wooden ladders came later.
gl.torno.name: The windlass
gl.torno.text: A wheel and rope over the shaft: it hauled up miners and ore much faster.
gl.jaula.name: The cage
gl.jaula.text: A lift for miners. In mines like the potash pits, it went down very deep at every shift.
gl.companeros.name: Workmates
gl.companeros.text: Miners looked after each other: if someone's light went out, the others went down to fetch them.
cave.1: You have reached the cave of the Green Men. Thousands of years ago it was a copper mine, and later the place where 35 people were laid to rest.
cave.2: In 1958, at Urbiola, their bones were found, stained green by the copper in the rock. That is why they are called the Green Men. Some are thought to have been metal seekers.
cave.3: Their work was hard, like that of every miner who came after them. Thanks to them there were tools, coins and fertiliser. Today we remember them.

up.pick.2.text: Blasters bored holes and filled them with powder

up.gear.1.name: Leather helmet
up.gear.2.name: Helmet and boots

up.ladders.1.name: Wooden ladders
up.ladders.2.name: Light ladders

fact.beriain: Beriáin was a village of 254 people. With the potash mine, from 1963, it became a mining town.
fact.encierro: In 1975 the potash miners stayed down the mine to ask for better conditions, and many people in Navarre joined them.
fact.arga: Eugi's magnesite was found in the 1940s, when someone spotted pieces of it in the river Arga.
fact.dolomita: The Eugi mine is famous around the world for its dolomite crystals, now kept in museums.
fact.milan: It is said that Philip II brought armourers from Milan to Eugi to make helmets and armour.
fact.orbaizeta: The Orbaizeta arms factory was founded in 1784, on the site of an ironworks from 1432.
fact.braccio: In 1362 a Florentine called Braccio ran the copper mine in the Arce valley.
fact.aia: About 2,000 years ago the Romans cut galleries by the Peñas de Aia, near Lesaka, for silver and lead.
fact.urbiola: The cave of the Green Men was found in 1958 at Urbiola, near Estella.
fact.ninos: For centuries children worked in mines too, carrying ore. Today the law forbids it.
fact.lampisteria: Mines had a lamp room, where the miners' lamps were looked after and handed out.
final.sub: You have dug down through thousands of years of Navarre's mines.
ben.shaft: Up the old shaft at {n} m a second
gl.casco.name: A miner's helmet
gl.casco.text: A helmet from the potash mine. Every shift, miners went down wearing one, with a lamp on the front.
gl.bala.name: A cannonball
gl.bala.text: The Eugi factory made ammunition for the king's army from the iron of these hills.
gl.dinero.name: A medieval coin
gl.dinero.text: The kings of Navarre made coins of silver. That is why the mines mattered so much to them.
fact.plantilla: At the end of 1974, 2,200 people worked at Potasas de Navarra.
fact.sellado: The potash galleries, all joined to each other, were sealed in the early 1990s.
fact.europa: Today more than half of Navarre's magnesite is sold to other European countries.
fact.eugipueblo: The Eugi factory was like a town: about 700 people, with a school, a doctor and a chapel.
fact.convencion: French soldiers destroyed the Eugi factory in 1794, in the War of the Convention.
fact.ruinas: The Orbaizeta factory closed in 1884. Its ruins still stand in the woods by the Irati forest.
fact.blanca: In 1432 Queen Blanca of Navarre allowed the iron, silver and lead of the Aezkoa valley to be worked.
fact.girardi: In 1340 a report said Navarre's copper and silver mines lay by Gipuzkoa and in the Arce valley.
fact.betelu: In the 16th and 17th centuries mines opened at Betelu, Imízcoz and Urrobi, mostly for iron.
fact.gorramendi: On Gorramendi, in Baztan, traces remain of how the Romans searched for gold.
fact.arditurri: The Roman galleries by the Peñas de Aia were worked from Roman times until the late 20th century.
fact.azurita: At the Urbiola cave, malachite and azurite were dug out: green and blue copper minerals.
